subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: A student writes a speech to convince classmates to start a school recycling scheme. What is the main purpose of this persuasive writing?
options: To describe a place in detail
To convince the audience to agree or act
To tell a story with a twist
To list facts with no opinion
questions.explanation: Persuasive writing aims to change what the audience thinks or does. Description, storytelling and neutral listing have different main purposes.

questions.content: Which sentence is the strongest example of a rhetorical question used to persuade?
options: The litter is on the playground.
I picked up the litter on Monday.
Litter is rubbish left in public places.
How long will we ignore the litter on our own playground?
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not to get an answer, and it pushes the reader to agree. The other options are plain statements.

questions.content: In the rule of three, a writer says: "Our town needs a safer, cleaner, greener park." What is the effect of the three adjectives?
options: They create rhythm and make the point feel complete
They confuse the reader with detail
They show that the writer is unsure
They turn the sentence into a question
questions.explanation: A list of three builds rhythm and sounds memorable and balanced. It does not add confusion or doubt.

questions.content: Which statement is a fact rather than an opinion?
options: The new bike lane is a wonderful idea
Everyone loves the new bike lane
The new bike lane is 2.4 kilometres long
The bike lane will obviously fix traffic
questions.explanation: A fact can be checked and proven. The other three are judgements or predictions presented as certain.

questions.content: What does the term 'call to action' mean at the end of a persuasive text?
options: A summary of the writer's life story
A direct request telling the reader what to do next
A quotation from a famous person
A description of the setting
questions.explanation: A call to action ends the text by asking the audience to act, for example 'Sign the petition today'.

questions.content: Read this invented opening: "Imagine walking to school and finding your favourite bench gone, replaced by a car park." Which technique does the writer use first?
options: A statistic from an official report
An expert quotation
A formal definition
A hook that invites the reader to picture a scene
questions.explanation: The word 'Imagine' invites the reader into a scene to grab attention. No numbers, expert or definition appear in the sentence.

questions.content: A writer says, "Every other school in the district already has a library café. Are we really going to be left behind?" Which appeal is used most strongly?
options: An appeal to the audience's fear of being left out
An appeal to scientific evidence
An appeal to the writer's qualifications
An appeal to tradition
questions.explanation: Comparing the school with others and suggesting it will be 'left behind' pushes an emotional reaction. No evidence or credentials are given.

questions.content: Which sentence uses ethos (credibility) to persuade?
options: Think of the tired faces on the morning bus
Studies show that sleep improves marks, so we must act
As a nurse for twenty years, I have seen what poor sleep does to teenagers
Sleep is vital, and you know it
questions.explanation: Ethos builds trust by showing the writer's experience or character. The second option is logos and the first is pathos.

questions.content: A writer claims: "Homework should be banned because it is boring." Which is the best way to strengthen the argument?
options: Repeat the word 'boring' three more times
Add evidence, such as a survey showing the effect of homework on sleep
Insult teachers who set homework
Remove the reason from the sentence
questions.explanation: A persuasive argument needs a reason supported by evidence. Repetition alone or insults do not build a convincing case.

questions.content: A speaker writes, "Some people may say the fee is too high, but the fee pays for new equipment." What is this technique called?
options: Alliteration
Hyperbole
Onomatopoeia
Addressing a counter-argument
questions.explanation: The writer names an opposing view and answers it, which makes the argument look fair and stronger. The other terms name sound or exaggeration devices.

questions.content: Which paragraph order best suits a persuasive essay?
options: Hook and clear position, reasons with evidence, counter-argument, strong conclusion
Conclusion, a random example, hook, evidence
Evidence only, then a story
Counter-argument only, then a joke
questions.explanation: A persuasive piece needs a clear position, supported reasons, a response to the other side and a firm ending. The other orders lack structure.

questions.content: Read this invented line: "Only a fool would ignore this offer." Why might this weaken a persuasive text for a mixed audience?
options: It uses too many statistics
It is written in the past tense
It insults readers who disagree, so they may stop listening
It is too polite
questions.explanation: Personal attack alienates the audience. Persuasion works better when it respects those who might disagree.

questions.content: A writer uses the phrase "a flood of plastic is drowning our beaches". Which device is used and why is it persuasive?
options: Simile, because it uses 'like'
Metaphor, because it makes the problem feel overwhelming
Rhyme, because the words sound alike
Understatement, because it plays the problem down
questions.explanation: The plastic is described as a flood without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor. The image makes the problem seem huge and urgent.

questions.content: Read this invented extract: "Our school wastes 400 plastic bottles a week. That is a mountain of rubbish, and it is not too late to stop it. Join the reuse challenge now!" Which choice best identifies the persuasive features in order?
options: Anecdote, simile, then rhetorical question
Expert quotation, alliteration, then question
Definition, irony, then a summary
Statistic, metaphor with hyperbole, then direct imperative call to action
questions.explanation: The number is a statistic, 'mountain of rubbish' is exaggerated imagery, and 'Join the reuse challenge now!' is a direct command. No anecdote or quotation appears.

questions.content: A student's persuasive letter has a strong hook and evidence but ends: "So, that is all I wanted to say." Which revision would improve it most?
options: Close by restating the position and adding a clear call to action
Add another statistic to the end only
Remove the hook
Make the ending shorter and less direct
questions.explanation: Persuasive pieces should end with force. The weak ending wastes the earlier work, so a restated position and call to action leaves the reader with something to do.

questions.content: An invented editorial says: "Since I started cycling, I have saved money. Therefore, all students should cycle to school." What is the main weakness?
options: The tone is too formal
It uses too many technical terms
A generalisation drawn from one personal experience
It lacks a title
questions.explanation: One person's experience does not prove a rule for everyone. A stronger version would give wider evidence.

questions.content: Writer A says: "Phones must be banned." Writer B says: "Phones should be limited in lessons, and a trial term would let us test the effect on results." Why might Writer B persuade a sceptical reader better?
options: It is shorter and so more powerful
The reasonable, specific proposal sounds fair and is easier to agree with
It uses fewer words that sound like a command
It avoids making any suggestion
questions.explanation: A balanced and specific proposal invites agreement from people who might reject an extreme claim. Writer B does make a suggestion, so the last option is wrong.

questions.content: An invented speech opens: "My grandmother crossed an ocean for a better school. Today we are asked to close ours." Which analysis is most accurate?
options: It is purely factual and avoids emotion
It uses a formal definition to persuade
It relies on a direct quotation from an expert
A personal anecdote builds pathos, and the contrast creates urgency
questions.explanation: The story of the grandmother is emotional and personal, and the contrast between her effort and the closure creates urgency. Nothing in the opening is a definition or quote.

note:
## What is persuasive writing?
Persuasive writing tries to make the reader agree with a point of view or take an action. Speeches, advertisements, letters to a newspaper, campaign posters and opinion blogs are all examples. In MYP Language and Literature you are asked to write persuasively and also to explain how other writers persuade, so you need to know the toolkit and how to use it with control.

## The three appeals
Writers often use three kinds of appeal. **Ethos** builds trust by showing the writer is knowledgeable, fair or experienced. **Pathos** appeals to emotion, such as pity, pride, fear or hope. **Logos** appeals to logic through facts, statistics, reasons and examples. The strongest pieces mix all three but never let emotion replace evidence.

## Techniques to use
- **Hook**: a strong opening, such as a question, a vivid scene or a surprising fact.
- **Rhetorical question**: a question asked for effect that pushes the reader towards your answer.
- **Rule of three**: a list of three items for rhythm, such as "safer, cleaner, greener".
- **Repetition**: repeating a key word or phrase so it sticks in the mind.
- **Emotive language**: words with strong feelings, such as "devastating" or "cherished".
- **Statistics and evidence**: numbers and examples that make your case credible.
- **Inclusive pronouns**: "we" and "our" make the reader feel on your side.
- **Imperatives**: commands such as "Join us" or "Sign today".

## Structure of a persuasive piece
1. A hook and a clear position.
2. Two or three developed reasons, each with evidence and explanation.
3. A counter-argument and your response to it. This shows fairness and strengthens your case.
4. A conclusion that restates your position and ends with a call to action.

## A short worked example
Position: "Our school should start a breakfast club." Reason: many students arrive hungry. Evidence: "In a survey of 60 students, 21 said they often skip breakfast." Explanation: "Hungry students find it harder to concentrate, so a club would help learning." Counter-argument: "Some say it will cost too much, but a small parent donation and volunteer helpers can cover it." That chain of point, evidence, explanation and response is the model to copy.

## Common mistakes
- Making a claim with no evidence, such as "Everyone knows this is true".
- Generalising from one example.
- Insulting people who disagree.
- Using so many techniques that the writing sounds forced.
- Forgetting the audience: a speech to students needs different language from a letter to a council.

## How this is examined
In the eAssessment-style tasks you may be given a short invented or real-style extract such as a campaign leaflet or a speech. You are then asked to state the purpose, identify techniques, explain their effect on the audience, and sometimes to plan or write your own persuasive piece. Marks reward naming the technique, quoting precisely and explaining the effect, not just spotting it.

Exam tip: Always follow the chain technique, quote, effect on the reader. Never just list devices.

flashcards.back: Writing designed to make the audience agree with a view or take an action.
An appeal to credibility and trust, shown through experience, expertise or fairness.
An appeal to the reader's emotions, such as sympathy, pride or fear.
An appeal to logic using facts, statistics, reasons and clear explanation.
A question asked for effect, not for an answer, to push the reader to agree.
Grouping three words or ideas together for rhythm and a sense of completeness.
A direct request at the end telling the reader what to do next.
An opposing view that a writer names and answers to appear fair and strengthen the case.
Words chosen to trigger strong feelings in the reader, such as 'devastating' or 'cherished'.

subject: english-language-and-literature

questions.content: What is the main aim of discursive writing?
options: To tell a story with characters
To persuade the reader with one view only
To describe a scene using the senses
To explore different sides of an issue in a balanced way
questions.explanation: Discursive writing discusses an issue from several angles. One-sided persuasion and storytelling are different purposes.

questions.content: Which linking phrase best introduces an opposing viewpoint?
options: On the other hand,
Furthermore,
In addition,
Similarly,
questions.explanation: 'On the other hand' signals a contrast. The other three add to or match an earlier point.

questions.content: Which sentence is written in a balanced, formal tone?
options: Uniforms are rubbish and everyone knows it
Uniforms are totally amazing, no question
Some people believe uniforms improve discipline, while others argue they limit self-expression
I reckon uniforms are okay, I guess
questions.explanation: A balanced tone presents both sides without slang or extreme claims.

questions.content: A discursive essay usually ends with:
options: A new unrelated topic
A reasoned conclusion that weighs the arguments
A joke about the reader
A list of unanswered questions only
questions.explanation: The conclusion should sum up the main arguments and give a considered judgement, even when the writer stays balanced.

questions.content: Which word hints that a writer is being cautious rather than absolute?
options: Always
Never
Everyone
Often
questions.explanation: 'Often' leaves room for exceptions. 'Always', 'never' and 'everyone' are absolute and need strong proof.

questions.content: A student plans an essay on whether teenagers should have part-time jobs. Which plan best shows a discursive approach?
options: Benefits, drawbacks, other factors, then a judged conclusion
Only the benefits, repeated three times
A story about a first job
A list of job adverts
questions.explanation: A discursive plan explores several sides and then reaches a reasoned view.

questions.content: Read this invented sentence: "Online lessons offer flexibility; however, they can leave some students feeling isolated." What does 'however' do?
options: It repeats the earlier idea
It gives the cause of the earlier idea
It introduces a contrast with the previous idea
It begins a conclusion
questions.explanation: 'However' signals a contrast between flexibility and isolation. It is not a repetition or a cause.

questions.content: Which sentence presents evidence in a balanced way?
options: Most students love shorter days
A survey of 120 students found that 70 preferred shorter days, though 50 favoured the current timetable
Nobody wants to keep the timetable
Surveys prove shorter days are best
questions.explanation: It gives numbers for both views. The others use absolute or unsupported claims.

questions.content: Which phrase shows a writer weighing the importance of arguments?
options: The cost is a number
Health is a word
Costs and benefits exist
While the cost matters, the long-term health benefits carry more weight
questions.explanation: Weighing means judging which point matters more and saying why. The other options only mention ideas.

questions.content: In a discursive essay on screen time, which topic sentence is best for the second body paragraph?
options: However, too much screen time can harm sleep and concentration
Screens are shiny
Many people have phones
This essay is about screens
questions.explanation: A good topic sentence states the paragraph's main point and links to a different side of the issue.

questions.content: A student writes: "Zoos are cruel." As part of a balanced piece, what should come next?
options: The same claim in capital letters
A recipe
An acknowledgement that some zoos support conservation, then a judgement
A list of zoo names
questions.explanation: Balanced writing recognises counter-evidence and then weighs it.

questions.content: Which sentence best shows a modest, hedged claim?
options: This proves homework helps all students
This evidence suggests that homework may help some students
Homework is the only way to learn
Homework never works
questions.explanation: Hedging words such as 'suggests' and 'may' show careful, balanced reasoning.

questions.content: A paragraph gives three reasons for later start times and nothing about the other side. How should the writer improve it for a discursive task?
options: Delete two of the reasons only
Make the language more emotional
Add a longer introduction only
Add at least one opposing view and compare it fairly
questions.explanation: A discursive piece needs more than one side. Adding and weighing an opposing view fixes the main gap.

questions.content: Read this invented extract: "Supporters of a four-day school week claim it reduces stress. Critics counter that longer days would tire younger children. Given the lack of local data, a trial seems the most sensible step." Which statement best describes the writer's approach?
options: Balanced: it presents both views and then proposes a measured action
One-sided: it supports only critics
Descriptive: it paints a scene
Narrative: it follows a plot
questions.explanation: Both supporters and critics are shown, and the writer draws a cautious conclusion based on missing data.

questions.content: A writer concludes: "There are strong arguments on both sides, so no decision can ever be made." Why is this a weak conclusion?
options: It uses a quotation
It is too detailed
It avoids weighing the arguments and reaches no judgement
It is in the wrong tense
questions.explanation: A discursive conclusion can be balanced, but it should still weigh the evidence and arrive at a reasoned position.

questions.content: Which revision best fixes this invented sentence: "Cars are bad, and they are good because they help people."?
options: Cars are bad but good
Cars bring convenience to many people; nevertheless, they add to pollution and congestion
Cars: good, bad
Cars help, they are bad
questions.explanation: The revision clarifies the contrast with a linking adverb and names each side precisely.

questions.content: A discursive essay about city cycling includes: a paragraph on health benefits, a paragraph on safety risks, a paragraph on the cost of lanes, then a conclusion that says 'cycling should be encouraged where lanes are safe'. Which feature makes the conclusion convincing?
options: It repeats the introduction word for word
It introduces a new, unsupported point
It avoids reference to evidence
It draws on all earlier paragraphs and sets a condition
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion links back to the arguments and gives a reasoned, qualified judgement.

questions.content: Writer X: "Many experts argue social media harms teenagers." Writer Y: "Research of 3,000 teenagers found a small link between heavy use and low mood, but the study could not prove cause." Which is the better discursive evidence and why?
options: Y, because it gives specific data and acknowledges a limit
X, because it sounds more confident
X, because it mentions experts
Y, because it avoids numbers
questions.explanation: Y has a sample size and recognises that correlation does not prove cause. X uses vague 'many experts' with no detail.

note:
## What is discursive writing?
Discursive writing explores an issue from more than one angle. Instead of shouting one opinion, you discuss arguments for and against, weigh them, and reach a reasoned judgement. Typical titles ask: "Should schools start later?" or "Is social media good for young people?". Discursive and balanced writing is common in essays, articles, reports and exam tasks.

## How it differs from persuasive writing
Persuasive writing pushes the reader towards one view. Discursive writing aims to inform and to examine. You can still give an opinion, but you must show that you have considered other positions fairly. The tone is calm, formal and measured. Words such as "perhaps", "may", "often" and "tends to" help you avoid sweeping claims.

## A reliable structure
1. **Introduction**: introduce the issue and why it matters. You may say you will look at both sides.
2. **Arguments for**: two or three points with evidence and explanation.
3. **Arguments against**: two or three points with evidence and explanation.
4. **Weighing**: a paragraph deciding which points are stronger and why.
5. **Conclusion**: a reasoned judgement that links back to the best evidence.

## Language for balance
- To add: furthermore, in addition, moreover.
- To contrast: however, on the other hand, nevertheless, whereas, while.
- To concede: admittedly, it is true that, although.
- To weigh: the most significant factor is, this outweighs, to a greater extent.
- To conclude: on balance, overall, in the end.

## A short worked example
Question: "Should phones be allowed in class?" A balanced paragraph could say: "Supporters point out that phones allow quick research and can help students who need translation tools. However, notifications interrupt concentration, and a study cannot easily show that every use is educational. On balance, phones are most useful when the teacher controls when they are used." Notice that it names both sides, uses linking words, includes a judgement and avoids saying "always" or "never".

## Common mistakes
- Presenting only one side while claiming to be balanced.
- Using extreme words such as "everyone", "nobody" or "always" without proof.
- Listing arguments but never weighing them.
- Finishing with "it depends" and no explanation.
- Using slang or a chatty tone.

## How this is examined
In the on-screen tasks you may be given two short invented extracts that give different opinions on a topic, and then asked to compare them or to plan a balanced response. You may be asked which language shows balance, how a writer qualifies a claim, or how a conclusion should weigh evidence. Marks reward clear structure, fair coverage of the sides, precise evidence and a reasoned judgement.

Exam tip: After you present two sides, always add a weighing sentence that begins "On balance" or "The stronger argument is".

flashcards.back: Writing that explores several sides of an issue, weighs the arguments and reaches a reasoned judgement.
A calm, formal voice that treats opposing views fairly, avoiding extreme or insulting language.
Cautious words such as 'may', 'often' or 'suggests' that avoid claiming too much.
Words such as however, nevertheless, whereas and on the other hand that show opposing ideas.
Admitting that an opposing point has some truth, for example 'It is true that...'.
Judging which points are stronger and explaining why, often with 'On balance'.
Introduction, points for, points against, weighing, reasoned conclusion.
Discursive explores both sides; persuasive pushes one view to change the reader's mind.
One that adds a new point, repeats the introduction word for word or refuses to judge the arguments.

subject: english-language-and-literature
subTopic: Formal Writing: Letters, Reports and Speeches

questions.content: In the UK and many other countries, how should a formal letter to a person whose name you do not know begin?
options: Dear Sir or Madam,
Hey there,
Hi mate,
To whom it may concern!!!
questions.explanation: A formal letter to an unknown reader uses a polite, standard greeting such as 'Dear Sir or Madam'. Casual greetings are unsuitable.

questions.content: If a formal letter begins 'Dear Sir or Madam,' how should it normally end?
options: Yours sincerely,
See you soon,
Yours faithfully,
Lots of love,
questions.explanation: The common convention is 'Yours faithfully' when you do not know the name and 'Yours sincerely' when you do.

questions.content: Which sentence is most suitable for a formal report?
options: Loads of students reckon a later start is awesome
The survey indicates that most students prefer a later start
Obviously, everyone hates mornings
Mornings are the worst, honestly
questions.explanation: A report uses objective, formal language based on evidence. The others are slangy or exaggerated.

questions.content: What is the purpose of a heading in a report?
options: To make the report longer
To show the writer's feelings
To add decoration
To organise information so the reader can find it quickly
questions.explanation: Reports use headings and subheadings to make the structure clear and help readers navigate.

questions.content: A speech is written to be:
options: Heard by an audience
Read silently on a page only
Sent as a text message only
Filed in a cabinet
questions.explanation: Speeches are spoken, so they use features such as direct address, rhythm, repetition and short sentences.

questions.content: A student writes to the principal: "Dear Mr Okoye, I am writing to propose a quiet study room during lunch." Which feature of formal letters is shown?
options: A closing slogan
A set of emoji
A clear opening purpose statement
An informal anecdote
questions.explanation: The first line states why the letter is being written, which is typical of formal letters.

questions.content: Which revision makes this sentence more formal? "We want a better canteen, it's rubbish now."
options: We want it better, ok?
We would like the canteen to be improved, as the current provision is inadequate
Fix the canteen soon
Canteen: bad, make good
questions.explanation: Formal writing avoids contractions and slang and uses complete, polite sentences.

questions.content: A report on school litter includes the sections: Introduction, Findings, Recommendations. Where would a suggestion such as 'install three extra bins by the sports field' belong?
options: Introduction
Findings
Title
Recommendations
questions.explanation: Recommendations propose actions based on the findings. The findings section reports what was discovered.

questions.content: Read this invented line from a speech: "We came. We saw. We cleaned." Which techniques does it use?
options: Short sentences and a pattern of three
Long complex sentences and a metaphor
Rhyming couplets and irony
Formal passive voice only
questions.explanation: Three short parallel sentences create rhythm that is easy to hear and remember, which suits speeches.

questions.content: Which opening is best for a speech delivered to a school assembly?
options: To whom it may concern.
The following report details packaging.
Good morning, everyone. Have you ever wondered what happens to your lunch packaging?
Dear Sir or Madam.
questions.explanation: A spoken opening greets the audience and hooks them, often with a question. The other options belong to letters or reports.

questions.content: A report writer says: "It is recommended that a trial be introduced." Which feature is shown?
options: First-person emotion
Passive voice to sound objective
Slang for humour
A rhetorical question
questions.explanation: The passive 'be introduced' keeps the tone impersonal and formal, which is common in reports.

questions.content: A formal complaint letter should usually:
options: Insult the recipient
Hide the problem
Avoid any request
State the problem, give details and ask for a specific action
questions.explanation: A good formal letter explains the issue clearly, supports it with details and says what the writer wants to happen.

questions.content: A speech about road safety includes: "Not one more child. Not one more family. Not one more day." Which technique is mainly used?
options: Anaphora (repetition at the start of each sentence)
Alliteration only
Onomatopoeia
Personification
questions.explanation: 'Not one more' begins each sentence, a repeated pattern called anaphora. It gives force and rhythm.

questions.content: Read this invented extract from a letter to a local council: "I am writing regarding the broken streetlight on Mill Lane, which has been out since 4 March. Several residents have reported near misses. I would be grateful if you would arrange a repair within two weeks." Which comment is most accurate?
options: It is vague and gives no purpose
It uses slang to build friendship
It states the issue, adds evidence and makes a polite, specific request
It ends with a rhetorical question
questions.explanation: The letter identifies the problem and date, gives evidence of danger and asks for a deadline politely.

questions.content: A student's report conclusion says: "We had a lot of fun and I think the survey was cool." Which weakness is most serious?
options: Too many headings
Informal, subjective language and no link to the findings
It is too long
It uses technical terms
questions.explanation: A report conclusion should be objective and based on evidence. The comment is casual and unrelated to results.

questions.content: A speaker is persuading a council to fund a skate park. Which version works best when spoken aloud?
options: The aforementioned recreational facility would, subject to budgetary constraints, be advantageous
Skate park: yes please, thanks, bye
Please consult appendix 4 for details of the facility
Picture a place where every young person belongs. Picture it. Then fund it
questions.explanation: Short, rhythmic, directly addressed sentences and repetition work well when heard. The other options are stiff, careless or meant for a document.

questions.content: A report says: "Of 80 students surveyed, 52 supported a later start." A writer wants to state the proportion accurately. Which statement is correct?
options: Exactly 65% of those surveyed supported a later start
Roughly 52% of those surveyed supported it
Exactly 80% supported it
Most of the 52 opposed it
questions.explanation: 52 ÷ 80 = 0.65, which is 65%. The other options misreport the data.

questions.content: An invented headteacher writes both a letter to parents and a speech to students about a new phone policy. Which choice describes how the register should differ?
options: Both must use identical wording
The speech should use technical report language
The letter is more formal and detailed; the speech is more direct, rhythmic and uses 'we'
The letter should be written in slang
questions.explanation: Different audiences and modes need different style. Letters are read and can be detailed. Speeches are heard and need clarity, rhythm and direct address.

note:
## Why formal writing matters
Formal writing is writing for a serious purpose and an audience you may not know well. In Language and Literature you may need to write letters, reports and speeches, and you may also be asked to analyse them. The skill is to match the form, the tone and the purpose, so that the reader takes you seriously.

## Formal letters
A formal letter has a clear layout and a polite, direct tone.
- **Sender's address and date** at the top.
- **Greeting**: "Dear Mr Okoye," if you know the name or "Dear Sir or Madam," if you do not.
- **Opening paragraph**: say why you are writing, for example "I am writing to complain about..." or "I am writing to propose...".
- **Body paragraphs**: give the details, evidence and reasons.
- **Final paragraph**: state what you want to happen and thank the reader.
- **Closing**: "Yours sincerely," after a named greeting or "Yours faithfully," after "Dear Sir or Madam,".
Avoid contractions, slang and exclamation marks.

## Reports
A report presents information clearly and objectively, usually for a decision maker. Typical sections are a **title**, **introduction** (purpose), **findings** (what you discovered, often with figures), **conclusion** and **recommendations** (what should happen next). Use headings and bullet points where they help. The language is impersonal: "It was found that..." or "The survey shows...". Support claims with data, and avoid your own feelings.

## Speeches
A speech is written to be heard. The audience cannot re-read, so you need clear structure and memorable sound.
- **Greet and hook** the audience.
- Use **direct address**: "you", "we", "our".
- Use **repetition**, **rule of three** and **short sentences** for rhythm.
- Use **rhetorical questions** to involve listeners.
- Signpost the structure: "My first point is..."
- End with a strong **call to action** or memorable line.

## Register and audience
Register is the level of formality. A letter to a council uses polite, formal language. A speech to classmates can be warmer but still controlled. Always ask: Who is the reader or listener? What do I want them to do or understand?

## A short worked example
Task: write to the principal about a shortage of lockers. Opening: "I am writing to request additional lockers for Year 10." Body: "A survey of 70 students found that 45 have nowhere to store bags, which causes congestion." Ending: "I would be grateful if you would consider a trial of 30 extra lockers. Yours sincerely, Amira Haddad." Here the purpose, evidence and request are all visible.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing formal and casual language.
- Wrong closing, such as "Yours faithfully" after a named greeting.
- Reports that give opinions without evidence.
- Speeches written as dense paragraphs that are hard to listen to.

## How this is examined
Exam-style tasks may provide a short invented extract such as a letter or speech and ask you to identify its form and purpose, explain how tone suits its audience, or plan your own response. You are marked on matching conventions, choosing suitable language and organising ideas clearly.

Exam tip: Before you write, note the form, audience and purpose in one line. It keeps your register consistent.

flashcards.back: A serious, polite style with no slang, few or no contractions and complete sentences.
Closing for a formal letter that begins 'Dear Sir or Madam,' when the name is unknown.
Closing for a formal letter that begins with a named greeting, such as 'Dear Ms Rao,'.
The opening line of a formal letter explaining why you are writing, e.g. 'I am writing to propose...'.
Title, introduction, findings, conclusion and recommendations, often with headings.
Suggested actions in a report, based on the findings.
Objective language, often using the passive voice, such as 'It was found that...'.
Speaking straight to the audience with words such as 'you', 'we' and 'our'.
Repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive sentences, common in speeches.
